messages.author: f0765d7b6293d9d6
messages.subject: 2-method sampling and using unmarked
parts:
Hi Everyone,

Please excuse me if this question has already been asked but I cannot find it through keyword searching,

My data collection involved 8 visits per site. 4 of which involved trapping, 4 of which involved underwater visual species identification. I have looked at both sampling methods using occu() and pcount() thanks to the great documentation and information on this forum.

I would next like to compare these two methodologies based on their estimated occupancy and detection (with covariates included). From what I can see I have 3 options:

1. Compare individual occu() results (trap vs. visual).
2. Run occu() where there is a siteCov of "sample method".
3. There is a built in method in unmarked that I am unaware of. (I have heard this before from someone but am not seeing anything that rings a bell)

My gut feeling is leaning towards method 1. However for many of my species, there is 0 trap catch and >>0 visual identifications. Perhaps reporting "0 catch" vs "0.36 visual detection probability" etc. is good enough and I am making this too complicated in these cases.

Thanks for any input anyone has on this!

Eric

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: 2-method sampling and using unmarked
parts:
Hi Eric,

1).  If the purpose is to compare these two methods, then I think you don't want to use option 1, because psi/z will be method specific and potentially very different, thus defeating the purpose of comparison.  

2).  Regarding option #2: do you mean sampling covariate? If different sampling methods were used at each site (such that you trapped one week, and snorkeled around another week) I think treating method as a visit covariate would be very reasonable.  If a site was sampled using trapping or visual id exclusively, then the comparison seems a little more tenuous to me, but I think using method as a site covariate for p might be your best option.

3).  If these different sampling methods were simultaneously occurring in slightly different patch subunits, multi-method or multi-scale models (Nichols et al. 2008, journal of applied ecology) might be a good option.  If the methods were sampling exactly the same place at the same time (i.e., independence of observations seems unlikely), then the Nichols et al. model might not appropriately describe the variance, but I think this would still be your best bet.   

Just my 0.02.  I would be curious to hear anybody else's take on using method as a site-covariate for p.  

Cheers,

John

messages.author: f0765d7b6293d9d6
messages.subject: Re: 2-method sampling and using unmarked
parts:
Hi John,

Thanks for your reply!

1) This explanation makes sense and I can see why this would not be a fair comparison.

2) You are right, I "mistyped" i meant sample covariate or obsCovs in unmarked. At each site, 4 traps were set (10m apart) and was coupled with a visual observation. I do agree with you that this probably suggests using method as a visit covariate could work well. I think for my purposes the effect of method on detection probability will be my most important conclusion here.
I was initially thinking of taking this another step and looking at how habitat characteristics affect the relationship between sampling methods (e.g. visual is more effective in open habitats and trapping in highly vegetated habitats). I am now realizing that this question can most likely not be answered by my sampling protocol and data, especially since this sampling method section is just an interesting side project.

3) Thanks for the link to this paper, it definitely looks relevant however I will need to spend more time with it.

Thanks again for the response. I appreciate the time you took to give me a full explaination.

Eric
